title: Problem Overview: Primes in (k, 2k) Avoiding Products
content: Erdos Problem #451 studies the function **n_k**, the smallest integer n > 2k such that the descending product (n-1)(n-2)...(n-k) has **no prime factor** in the interval (k, 2k). By **Bertrand's postulate**, such primes always exist, making avoidance non-trivial. The problem asks for the **precise growth rate** of n_k: it should grow faster than any polynomial (**superpolynomial**) yet slower than any exponential (**sub-exponential**).
mathContext: The connection to Bertrand's postulate is key: for every k >= 1, there is at least one prime p with k < p < 2k. Avoiding all such primes as factors of a product of k consecutive shifted integers requires a delicate number-theoretic construction. The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) reduces the problem to finding a simultaneous residue class that avoids dangerous residues modulo each Bertrand-range prime.
prerequisites: Bertrand's postulate on primes between k and 2k
asymptotic growth rates: polynomial vs exponential

title: Descending Product
content: **descendingProduct n k** computes the product (n-1)(n-2)...(n-k) as a finite product over the index set {1, ..., k}. This product captures k consecutive integers ending just below n, and its **prime factorization** drives the entire problem.
mathContext: Among k consecutive integers, the distribution of prime factors is governed by the principle that a prime p divides at most floor(k/p) + 1 of them. For primes p > k, at most one factor in the product is divisible by p, which is the key structural insight exploited in the CRT analysis.
prerequisites: the count of multiples of a prime in an interval

title: Bertrand Prime Avoidance
content: **AvoidsBertrandPrimes n k** asserts that no prime p in the interval (k, 2k) divides the descending product. The predicate **IsInBertrandRange** captures the three conditions: k < p, p < 2k, and p is prime. This is the central feasibility condition defining which n values are valid.
mathContext: The avoidance condition is equivalent to requiring that for every Bertrand-range prime p, the value n does not fall into any of the k 'dangerous' residue classes modulo p. Since k < p, these k residue classes {1, 2, ..., k} mod p are all distinct, leaving exactly p - k 'safe' residues per prime.

title: The Function n_k (Axiomatized)
content: The function **nk** is axiomatized with three properties: (1) **nk k > 2k** ensures we look beyond the trivial range; (2) **nk_avoids** confirms it satisfies the Bertrand avoidance condition; (3) **nk_minimal** ensures it is the **smallest** such value. Together these uniquely characterize n_k.
mathContext: Axiomatizing nk rather than computing it is necessary because determining n_k exactly requires an exhaustive search through residue systems. The known computed values (n_1 = 3, n_2 = 6, ..., n_10 = 220) grow rapidly and irregularly, suggesting the function's behavior is governed by the arithmetic structure of Bertrand-range primes.

title: CRT Structural Lemmas
content: Three key structural results formalize the **Chinese Remainder Theorem** perspective: (1) **at_most_one_div** shows that for a prime p > k, at most one of the k factors n-1, ..., n-k is divisible by p; (2) **prime_dvd_descendingProduct** gives the equivalence between p dividing the product and p dividing some factor; (3) **card_safeResidues** counts exactly **p - k safe residue classes** modulo each prime p in (k, 2k).
mathContext: The at_most_one_div lemma is the combinatorial heart: if p divides both (n - i) and (n - j), then p divides |i - j|. But 1 <= i, j <= k and k < p, so |i - j| < p, forcing i = j. This means avoiding p as a factor of the product reduces to avoiding a single residue class per factor, and the safe residues form the set {0, k+1, k+2, ..., p-1} of cardinality p - k.
prerequisites: prime divisibility of differences of integers
counting safe residue classes modulo a prime

title: Erdos-Graham Lower Bound
content: The **Erdos-Graham lower bound** states that n_k > k^(1+c) for some absolute constant c > 0 and all sufficiently large k. This shows the growth rate is **strictly superlinear** -- stronger than the trivial bound n_k > 2k but far from exponential.
mathContext: The proof relies on counting arguments in the sieve-theoretic framework. The number of 'safe' residues per prime p in (k, 2k) is p - k, which by Bertrand's postulate is at most k - 1. The density of safe integers decreases as the product of (p - k)/p over all Bertrand-range primes, and the prime number theorem shows this product decays polynomially faster than 1/k, yielding the superlinear lower bound.
prerequisites: sieve methods and density of safe integers

title: Adenwalla Upper Bound via CRT
content: **Adenwalla's upper bound** shows n_k <= product of all primes in (k, 2k), which is e^(O(k)) by the prime number theorem. The proof idea is explicit: take n = 0 mod p for every Bertrand-range prime p. By the **Chinese Remainder Theorem**, such an n exists and equals the product of those primes. The theorem **adenwalla_crt_idea** formalizes this reduction, showing that if M = prod(bertrandPrimes k) satisfies the avoidance condition, then nk k <= M by minimality.
mathContext: By the prime number theorem, the sum of log p over primes p in (k, 2k) is asymptotically k, so the product of these primes is e^(k + o(k)). This gives an explicit exponential upper bound. The gap between the superlinear lower bound k^(1+c) and the exponential upper bound e^(O(k)) is precisely what Problem 451 seeks to resolve.
prerequisites: the primorial and Chebyshev's theorem on prime products
the prime number theorem for sums of log p

title: Trivial Lower Bound (Proved)
content: The theorem **nk_trivial_lower** is the one fully proved result: n_k > 2k follows immediately from the axiom nk_gt_2k by casting from natural numbers to rationals. This is the baseline bound that all deeper results strengthen.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of trivial lower bound (proved)
prerequisites: coercion from natural numbers to rationals

title: Erdos Problem 451: Superpolynomial but Sub-exponential
content: The conjecture is split into two parts: (1) **ErdosProblem451_superpolynomial** asserts n_k > k^d for every constant d and all sufficiently large k; (2) **ErdosProblem451_subexponential** asserts n_k < 2^(epsilon * k) for every epsilon > 0 and all sufficiently large k. Together they place n_k in the **intermediate growth regime** between polynomial and exponential -- a rare and interesting phenomenon in combinatorial number theory.
mathContext: Functions with superpolynomial but sub-exponential growth occupy a narrow band in the hierarchy of growth rates. Classic examples include e^(sqrt(k)) and e^(k / log k). The conjecture implies n_k belongs to this class, and determining its precise asymptotic (e.g., whether n_k ~ e^(c * sqrt(k * log k)) for some c) remains completely open.
prerequisites: the hierarchy of asymptotic growth classes
intermediate growth in combinatorial number theory
